When the population standard deviation (σ) is known, use the normal distribution; when it is unknown and estimated by the sample standard deviation (s), use the Student t-distribution with degrees of freedom df = n – 1. The degrees of freedom determine the specific shape of the t-distribution curve, which has thicker tails than the normal distribution but approaches the normal shape as df increases.

To flag unusually low or high observations, calculate the Interquartile Range (IQR), which is the difference between the third quartile ($Q_3$) and first quartile ($Q_1$, representing the middle 50% of ordered data). Flag values below $Q_1 - 1.5 \times IQR$ or above $Q_3 + 1.5 \times IQR$.

Count-based outcomes (discrete random variables) take only finite or countably infinite distinct values, typically whole numbers resulting from a count of items like cars in a parking lot; measurement-based outcomes (continuous random variables) can take any value within an interval, such as the weight of apples. The contexts do not use the specific terms "count-based" and "measurement-based," but they define discrete variables as results of counts with distinct values and continuous variables as results of measurements taking any value in a range.
